title: What Is Human Capital Management (HCM)?
summary: Human capital management (HCM) is essential to optimizing HR functions. Read how the right HCM tools support your people and operations.
body_text: Human capital management is a critical business function that centers on optimizing the value of an organization’s employees. Essentially, HCM is the comprehensive set of practices and tools used to recruit, manage and develop a workforce. It treats employees as valuable assets and focuses on enhancing their skills, increasing their satisfaction and promoting their growth within the company. Effective human capital management strategies are pivotal to attracting top talent, fostering a productive work culture and driving organizational success. Below, we examine the components of HCM, how it differs from adjacent terms, its impact on employees and how to select the software that supports it. What is human capital management? Human capital management is the practice of managing the entire employee life cycle as a strategic investment. This includes a range of methods and tools used to attract, recruit, train, develop, manage and retain an effective workforce. HCM refers to both a business strategy and a category of software organizations use to manage their people from hire to retire. This covers everything from recruiting and payroll to benefits, performance and workforce planning, making it the broadest of the common HR technology categories. HCM vs. HR vs. HRIS vs. HRMS vs. talent management These terms overlap and are often used interchangeably, but each describes something distinct. HCM is the umbrella; the others are either narrower systems within it or the broader strategy it sits inside. Term What it covers How it relates to HCM Human resources (HR) Core administrative functions: hiring, job and position management, compliance, recordkeeping and reporting. The traditional, task-focused foundation. HCM is the strategic layer built on top HCM The full employee life cycle (recruiting, payroll, benefits, talent, performance and workforce planning), managed as a strategic investment. The umbrella strategy and software category. The broadest term here. Human resources information system (HRIS) The system of record for employee data: records, policies and core HR workflows. A core component within HCM; narrower and data-focused. See the difference between an HRIS and broader HCM . Human resource management system (HRMS) The applications that automate HR processes across the employee life cycle. Often used interchangeably with HCM software, HRMS emphasizes strategy over administration. Talent management Sourcing, performance, learning, career development and succession. A subset of HCM focused on developing and retaining people. SHRM frames it as integrating every stage of the employee life cycle into one strategy. Workforce management Time and labor, scheduling and absence management. A subset of HCM focused on time-based operations. For larger organizations weighing a system of record against a full HCM suite, see what an enterprise HRIS is and where it fits . What does human capital management include? Human capital management is a multifaceted operation, with several components working together to strengthen and optimize a workforce. Here are the essential HCM functions. Workforce planning Workforce planning is the strategic process of aligning a company’s human resources with its business goals. This is used to forecast future staffing needs, identify skills gaps and implement plans to find the right talent. The stakes are real: U.S. employers recorded roughly 5 million job separations in a single month . Without proactive planning, that churn turns into unfilled roles, lost institutional knowledge and reactive hiring. Recruiting and hiring Recruiting and hiring is the process of attracting, evaluating and selecting candidates to fill roles — a crucial step in building a skilled, diverse workforce that aligns with a company’s culture and vision. Benefits administration Benefits administration involves managing and delivering employee benefits, including health insurance, retirement plans and paid leave. This is not a minor line item: Benefits accounted for 30.1% of total compensation costs for private-industry employers. Solid benefits administration is key to attracting and retaining talent while accurately managing one of an employer’s largest cost categories. Payroll management Payroll management is the accurate, timely processing of employee compensation (wages, taxes and other deductions). In practice, that means handling real-world complexity: retroactive pay after a midcycle raise, off-cycle payments, multistate tax withholding for remote employees, shift differentials and wage garnishments. Getting these right protects payroll compliance and employee trust; getting them wrong invites penalties, rework and audit exposure. Training, learning and development, reporting and analytics, performance management, employee experience (EX) and compensation planning round out the core HCM functions. What are the benefits and challenges of human capital management? Human capital management delivers measurable organizational value, but it comes with real challenges, including competition in the labor market, high training costs, change management and the need to maintain engagement and retention. With the right strategy, organizations can maximize their workforce’s potential while streamlining essential HR functions. Key benefits include streamlining recruitment, identifying skills gaps, improving retention and boosting operational efficiency. Streamlining the recruitment process An effective HCM strategy increases the speed at which an organization can recruit and onboard prospective candidates. It streamlines the process by empowering hiring managers to easily manage and track applicants. Identifying skills gaps Human capital management helps businesses identify potential skills gaps in relation to their overall strategy. Organizations can create a proactive plan to source or develop talent to help fill in the gaps. Improving employee retention The right HCM strategy empowers employees to use their skills and training to reach their career goals. Employers have a better understanding of their workforce’s needs and can provide opportunities and training to help employees succeed. Boosting operational efficiency Ultimately, human capital management allows an organization to enhance its operational effectiveness, driving efficiency and productivity by meeting the needs of its employees. What is HCM software? Human capital management software is an integrated suite of tools designed to manage and optimize an organization’s HR processes from recruitment to retirement. By streamlining critical HR functions like talent acquisition, payroll, performance management and benefits administration, HCM software allows for data-driven decision-making and enhances the overall employee experience. How does HCM software help manage talent? Human capital management software offers a comprehensive suite of tools that streamline the entire employee life cycle, facilitating the attraction, retention and growth of talent within an organization. It also helps HR professionals efficiently: track performance set clear individual career paths develop and offer targeted training programs By centralizing these critical HR functions, HCM software helps create a cohesive strategy for talent management that ensures employees are skilled, engaged and prepared to meet future challenges. What size business requires HCM software? Human capital management software provides substantial benefits for businesses of all sizes, from startups to enterprise organizations. For small businesses, HCM software is a game changer. It automates and streamlines processes like payroll, benefits administration and employee onboarding, which can be challenging for smaller teams with limited resources. This leads to increased efficiency and accuracy, giving you more time to focus on strategically growing your business. HCM software also helps small companies manage compliance , reducing the risk of errors that often carry legal and financial penalties. And, critically, it provides a scalable solution that grows with the business, so your HR functions can adapt as your company expands. For organizations at enterprise scale, pairing HCM with the right system of record matters (see what an enterprise HRIS is ). 6 tips for selecting the right HCM software Use these six tips to identify and select the best HCM platform for your business. 1. Understand the differences in HR tech providers Each HCM provider has unique features, functionality and levels of customization that may or may not align with your specific business needs. You need HCM software that matches your company’s strategic objectives and can significantly enhance operational efficiency, user adoption rates and the overall return on investment. That’s why it’s crucial to discern all the nuances between providers, ensuring that your ultimate choice integrates smoothly with existing workflows and allows your business to scale its HR efforts efficiently. 2. Ease of use matters most for successful adoption An HCM platform’s ease of use directly impacts a workforce’s willingness to engage with the system. User-friendly interfaces and intuitive navigation ensure that all users, regardless of their technical proficiency, can efficiently complete tasks, access information and use the software’s full range of functionality. Accessible HCM software can lead to higher usage rates, less of a learning curve (and associated training costs), and higher productivity and satisfaction among your workforce. 3. HCM tech should help you positively impact culture and engagement Human capital management software plays a pivotal role in shaping employees’ day-to-day experiences — the building blocks of company culture. By facilitating transparent communication, recognizing achievements and offering easy access to professional development resources, HCM tech can enhance engagement and empower employees to do their best work. When people feel supported by the tools they use, it can drive a positive culture and increase the retention of top performers. 4. Choose technology that supports your employer brand, hiring strategy and employees’ careers Your HCM tech reflects your company’s commitment to providing a seamless and engaging employee experience — a direct extension of the employer brand . By enabling a strategic approach to hiring and fostering ongoing career development, the right human capital management tech can help your business attract candidates who resonate with your values while supporting the growth of current employees. This can bolster your organization’s reputation as an employer of choice and a nurturer of talent. 5. Be audit-ready Ensuring your business consistently complies with labor laws, tax regulations and industry standards is also critical. HCM software that facilitates easy access to accurate, comprehensive and up-to-date employee data dramatically simplifies the process of preparing for and undergoing audits. By being audit-ready, you’ll minimize the risk of noncompliance (and associated penalties) while reinforcing the integrity and reliability of your organization’s HR processes. In turn, you’ll improve the overall trust in your company from stakeholders and employees alike. 6. Do your due diligence Selecting a human capital management platform is a significant investment of time and resources, and the system you choose will profoundly impact your business’s operational efficiency. By being thorough in your evaluation, you can ensure that your chosen HCM platform: meets your current needs scales with future growth provides the necessary support and security This can go a long way toward avoiding costly mistakes (like investing in a system that fails to deliver on its promises or becomes quickly outdated), safeguarding your investment and sustaining long-term management of your workforce. For a current market view, see this comparison of HCM software in 2026 . How does Paycom support HCM strategy? Paycom supports HCM strategy through a truly single software to address all HR functions. This easy-to-use, comprehensive approach enhances data accuracy, efficiency, compliance and engagement, and supports better strategic planning as businesses can easily access and analyze critical workforce data. Moreover, Paycom’s emphasis on self-service tools empowers employees to manage their personal information, benefits and career development. By automating and simplifying HR tasks, Paycom allows businesses to focus less on administrative details and more on strategic initiatives to align human capital with business goals. The impact shows up in real numbers. After The Kraft Group (parent company of the New England Patriots, with 5,000 employees across 20 businesses in eight industries and five states) moved to Paycom, its HR team cut payroll prep time by 75% and grew employee usage of its HR tech to 100%. “We can complete payroll prep in just eight hours, instead of the 32 hours it took before Paycom,” said Lauren Melz, HR data and reporting manager. “Data is everything. Without Paycom, our world would be overwhelming. With Paycom’s full-solution automation, we’re on top of cost controls and efficiencies, and that drives the return on our investment,” said John Flaherty, senior vice president of operations at The Kraft Group. Human capital management: FAQ What is the difference between HR and HCM? HR takes a more traditional approach to workforce management, focusing primarily on the administrative functions of hiring, compensating and maintaining employees. HCM goes beyond the traditional functions of HR to develop, engage and optimize an organization’s talent and meets its overall objectives. What does a human capital management system do? A human capital management system offers a comprehensive suite of tools that streamline the entire employee life cycle. From recruiting potential candidates to fostering their professional development, HCM systems facilitate the attraction, retention and growth of talent within an organization. Why is human capital management important? In today’s ultra-competitive and rapidly changing business environment, effective human capital management helps organizations attract top talent, foster a productive work culture and drive organizational success. What does HCM stand for? HCM stands for human capital management, which is both the strategy and the software organizations use to manage the full employee life cycle, from hire to retire. What is HCM in HR? In an HR context, HCM is the strategic framework and supporting technology that turns administrative HR tasks into a coordinated approach to recruiting, developing, paying and retaining employees. What is the difference between HCM and HRIS? An HRIS is the system of record for employee data and core HR workflows. HCM is broader: It includes the HRIS plus payroll, benefits, talent and performance management as one strategic approach. Learn more about the role of an HRIS .

title: How Do I Move My Business From POTS to Cloud Communications?
summary: POTS lines are being retired nationwide. Here's how to move to cloud communications, from evaluating providers through go-live cutover.
body_text: TL;DR: Moving from POTS to cloud communications, whether you’re getting ahead of the shutdown or responding to a carrier’s notice, happens in four phases: evaluating providers, porting and provisioning numbers, testing and cutting over, and training your team after go-live. Most migrations take 30 to 90 days, depending on line count and how many systems still run on copper. In this post: What does the move from POTS to cloud communications actually involve? What should you look for in a cloud communications provider? How does number porting and provisioning actually work? What does cutover day look like, and how do you avoid downtime? How do you get your team ready to adopt the new system? Carriers across the country are retiring POTS (plain old telephone service) lines, the copper network that’s carried analog business phone calls for decades. Some businesses are moving proactively, ahead of any notice. Others are moving because a notice already arrived, with a firm disconnection date attached. Either way, once it’s time to leave copper behind, the question that matters most is how the move to cloud communications actually happens. (For the regulatory background on why this is happening now, see our overview of the POTS lines shutdown .) This post covers the mechanics of the move itself. A POTS-to-cloud migration isn’t one cutover event. It’s four connected phases: evaluating providers, porting and provisioning numbers, testing and cutting over, and training your team to use the new system. Skipping a phase, or rushing through it under deadline pressure, is where most migration problems start. Here’s what each phase involves and how to move through them without losing a business day of phone service. What Does the Move From POTS to Cloud Communications Actually Involve? A POTS-to-cloud migration moves through four phases: provider evaluation, number porting and provisioning, testing and cutover, and team training. Each phase depends on the one before it, so working out of order tends to create rework later. Treat the migration as four connected phases, not one weekend project. Provider evaluation comes first because it shapes every decision after it: which numbers can port, what hardware you’ll need, and how life-safety lines get replaced. Porting and provisioning follow once a provider is selected, moving your numbers and setting up your new cloud phone system in parallel with your existing copper lines. Testing and cutover come next, confirming call quality, routing, and emergency calling before the old lines go dark. Training closes the loop, since a technically successful migration still fails if employees don’t know how to use the new system. Most businesses underestimate how much of this work happens before the actual switch. A well-run migration spends more time on evaluation and provisioning than on cutover day itself. That sequencing is also why timelines vary so widely: a five-line office might complete all four phases in a few weeks, while a multi-location business with alarm panels and elevator lines on copper should plan for closer to 90 days. What Should You Look For in a Cloud Communications Provider? Look for a provider with a clear uptime commitment, documented e911 compliance, and a specific plan for replacing life-safety lines, not just standard voice service. A provider that treats fire alarms and elevator phones as an afterthought will make you find that out during an emergency, not before one. Reliability comes first: ask for the provider’s published uptime SLA and how outages are communicated, not just how they’re prevented. E911 compliance matters because cloud systems handle location data differently than copper lines did, and the provider should explain exactly how a call routes to first responders from each of your addresses. For life-safety lines specifically, ask whether the provider has a dedicated POTS replacement solution built for fire, security, and elevator systems, rather than a generic voice line repurposed for the job. Integration and support round out the list. Confirm the platform connects to the business tools your team already uses, and ask what support looks like during the migration itself, not just after go-live. Businesses that make the move tend to see it pay off: Metrigy’s 2026 research found that nearly six in ten companies now run cloud communications as their primary calling and collaboration platform , with analysts pointing to real productivity gains, not just lower costs, as the reason adoption keeps climbing. How Does Number Porting and Provisioning Actually Work? Number porting moves your existing phone numbers to your new provider through a formal request called a Letter of Authorization, then activates them on the new platform once the losing carrier releases them. Porting a phone number is usually the slowest step in the entire migration, not the fastest. The process starts with a Letter of Authorization, a signed document giving your new provider permission to request your numbers from your current carrier. From there, business number ports commonly take one to four weeks, depending on carrier responsiveness and how many numbers are involved. Mismatched account details, such as an address or account name that doesn’t exactly match the carrier’s records, are the most common cause of delay. Provisioning happens alongside porting: your new provider sets up extensions, call routing, and devices on the cloud platform before your numbers officially transfer. Running both systems in parallel during this window lets you test the new setup without disrupting the phone service your business depends on right now. Numbers that connect to fax lines, alarm monitoring, or other non-human systems often need separate attention here, since those connections don’t always port and provision the same way a standard desk phone does. What Does Cutover Day Look Like, and How Do You Avoid Downtime? Cutover day is when call traffic actually switches from your old POTS lines to your new cloud platform, and it goes smoothest when it’s staged and tested rather than flipped all at once. The businesses that avoid downtime are the ones that test everything before cutover day, not during it. Before cutover, run test calls in both directions, confirm caller ID displays correctly, and verify that emergency calls route to the right location. Staging the cutover by location or line group, rather than switching every line simultaneously, limits how much is exposed if something doesn’t work as expected. It’s also worth confirming with your provider what the rollback plan looks like: how quickly you could revert to copper if a critical issue surfaces in the first few hours. If a carrier’s notice has already set a deadline, that deadline doesn’t change what needs to happen before cutover, it just compresses how much time there is to do it. A shorter window is a reason to prioritize testing on your highest-risk lines first, not a reason to skip testing altogether. Businesses moving proactively, without a notice forcing the date, have more room to sequence this deliberately, but the same testing steps still apply. How Do You Get Your Team Ready to Adopt the New System? Getting your team ready means training on the specific tasks people do daily, documenting who to contact with issues, and collecting feedback in the first few weeks after go-live. A migration that goes technically well can still fail if nobody on your team knows how to transfer a call. Short, task-specific training beats a single long overview session. Show employees how to do the handful of things they actually do every day, like transferring calls or checking voicemail, rather than walking through every feature the platform offers. Pair that with simple written documentation they can reference later, since not everyone will remember a training session word for word. Naming an internal point of contact for questions in the first two weeks after go-live matters just as much as the training itself. That person can field small issues before they turn into larger frustrations, and can flag patterns back to your provider if the same question keeps coming up. Built-in feedback loops during this window help you catch adoption gaps early, while they’re still easy to fix. Ready to Move Off Copper? Whatever your current POTS lines connect to, Crexendo VIP can help you plan and execute the move to cloud communications without guessing at the details. SCHEDULE A DEMO FAQ How long does a POTS-to-cloud migration take? Most migrations take 30 to 90 days from provider selection to full cutover. Smaller offices with few lines can move faster; businesses with multiple locations or life-safety systems on copper should plan for the longer end of that range. Will my phone number change when I switch to cloud communications? No. Existing numbers typically port to the new provider through a Letter of Authorization process, so your business keeps the same numbers customers already know. Do I need new hardware for cloud communications? Not always. Many cloud phone systems support existing desk phones, or offer softphone apps that work on computers and mobile devices, so hardware needs depend on your provider and preferences. What happens to fire alarms and elevator phones during the migration? These life-safety lines need dedicated replacement devices built to emulate analog signals, not a standard voice line. Confirm your provider has a specific plan for these systems before cutover, not after. Can I migrate in phases instead of all at once? Yes. Staging cutover by location or line group is a common way to limit risk and catch issues on a smaller scale before moving the rest of your lines. GAAP earnings per share (EPS) increased 13% to $1.12 and adjusted EPS decreased 4% to $1.01. "Otis delivered a solid quarter, with net sales up 7%, supported by growth across all Service lines and sequential improvement in New Equipment trends. Our strategy, actions and investments in Service quality are gaining traction as evidenced by double-digit growth in both modernization and repair sales with maintenance growth also accelerating, contributing to Service sales growth that matched the highest level achieved since spin," said Chair, CEO & President Judy Marks. "Strong backlog in both modernization and New Equipment provides good visibility and supports our expectation for continued growth in the quarters ahead. We remain confident in the long-term growth opportunities across our Service portfolio. An aging installed base and our customers' increasing focus on reliability, uptime and Service quality are driving favorable demand in both modernization and repair, contributing to drive sustained growth and value creation." Judy Marks continued, "As we look to the second half of the year and take a measured approach to our outlook, we remain confident in the durability of our Service-led growth model. We are continuing to invest in our strategic priorities including Service quality, pricing initiatives, and the application of digital technology with a focus on front-line operating excellence and strong execution across the globe. This Service-driven strategy reinforces our conviction in the long-term growth potential of the business and our ability to deliver sustainable value creation for shareholders over time." Use and Definitions of Non-GAAP Financial Measures Otis Worldwide Corporation ("Otis") reports its financial results in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States ("GAAP"). We supplement the reporting of our financial information determined under GAAP with certain non-GAAP financial information. The non-GAAP information presented provides investors with additional useful information, but should not be considered in isolation or as substitutes for the related GAAP measures. Below are our non-GAAP financial measures: Non-GAAP measure Definition Organic sales Represents consolidated net sales (a GAAP measure), excluding the impact of foreign currency translation, acquisitions and divestitures completed in the preceding twelve months and other significant items of a non-recurring and/or nonoperational nature ("other significant items"). Management believes organic sales is a useful measure in providing period-to-period comparisons of the results of the Company's ongoing operational performance. Adjusted selling, general and administrative ("SG&A") expense Represents SG&A expense (a GAAP measure), excluding restructuring costs and other significant items. Adjusted operating profit Represents income from continuing operations (a GAAP measure), excluding restructuring costs and other significant items. Adjusted net interest expense Represents net interest expense (a GAAP measure), adjusted for the impacts of non-recurring acquisition related financing costs and related net interest expense pending the completion of a transaction and other significant items. Adjusted noncontrolling interest in earnings Represents noncontrolling interest in earnings (a GAAP measure), excluding restructuring costs and other significant items, including related tax effects. Adjusted net income Represents net income attributable to Otis Worldwide Corporation (a GAAP measure), excluding restructuring costs and other significant items, including related tax effects. Adjusted earnings per share ("EPS") Represents diluted earnings per share attributable to common shareholders (a GAAP measure), adjusted for the per share impact of restructuring and other significant items, including related tax effects. Adjusted effective tax rate Represents the effective tax rate (a GAAP measure) adjusted for other significant items and the tax impact of restructuring costs and other significant items. Constant currency GAAP financial results include the impact of changes in foreign currency exchange rates ("AFX"). We use the non-GAAP measure "at constant currency" or "CFX" to show changes in our financial results without giving effect to period-to-period currency fluctuations. Under U.S. GAAP, income statement results are translated in U.S. dollars at the average exchange rate for the period presented. Management believes that this non-GAAP measure is useful in providing period-to-period comparisons of the results of the Company's ongoing operational performance. Free cash flow Represents cash flow from operations (a GAAP measure) less capital expenditures. Management believes free cash flow is a useful measure of liquidity and an additional basis for assessing Otis' ability to fund its activities, including the financing of acquisitions, debt service, repurchases of common stock and distribution of earnings to shareholders. Free cash flow should not be considered an alternative to, or more meaningful than, net cash flows provided by operating activities, or any other measure of liquidity presented in accordance with GAAP. Adjusted free cash flow Represents cash flow from operations (a GAAP measure) less capital expenditures, adjusted to exclude certain items management believes affect the comparability of operating results. Management believes adjusted free cash flow is a useful measure of liquidity that provides investors additional information regarding the Company's ability to fund its activities, including the financing of acquisitions, debt service, repurchases of common stock and distribution of earnings to shareholders. Adjusted free cash flow should not be considered an alternative to, or more meaningful than, net cash flows provided by operating activities, or any other measure of liquidity presented in accordance with GAAP. title: How Red Ball Oxygen Stayed Family-Owned Through Consolidation
summary: Red Ball Oxygen made MDM's 2025 Top Distributors list in Gases & Welding Supplies. How a Shreveport family business held its ground as the vertical rolled up.
body_text: Part of Distributor Playbooks — strategy teardowns of every company on the 2025 MDM Top Distributors lists . In railroad slang, a "red ball" shipment was the one that jumped the queue: priority freight, moved fast, tagged for expedited handling. A Louisiana company borrowed the term in 1930 and has spent the better part of a century trying to live up to it. Red Ball Oxygen Co. shows up on the 2025 MDM Top Distributors list in Gases & Welding Supplies, one of twenty verticals Modern Distribution Management tracks across North America's largest wholesale distributors. MDM doesn't disclose a revenue figure for Red Ball, which is itself a data point: this is a private, family-run company that has never needed to court public investors, and its own history explains why. The business it almost wasn't Red Ball's 1930 incorporation is a technicality more than an origin story. The company that actually matters was born in 1969, when Craig and Lorena Kennedy bought a struggling outfit called Red Ball Battery and Oxygen. At the time it was a National Cylinder Gas distributor selling automotive batteries and tires, with four employees and a single location, according to a company history published by GAWDA's trade media arm . The batteries-and-tires business was not the future. Welding gas was. The Kennedys made the pivot: out of automotive retail, into industrial and specialty gas, cylinder fill, and welding supply. That single bet is the entire company today. By its 50th anniversary in 2019, Red Ball had grown to roughly 235 employees, three cylinder fill plants in Shreveport, Houston, and Dallas, two specialty gas plants, and 23 retail locations across a four-state footprint. The company's own about-us page puts the current network at more than 20 customer service locations and four fill plants spanning Louisiana, Texas, Arkansas, and Oklahoma, with a newly opened Port Arthur branch extending the map further into the Gulf Coast petrochemical corridor. Three generations of Kennedys have now run the company. Alex Kennedy holds the chairman and CEO title; Larry Kennedy chairs the board; Bob Ewing serves as president. That succession, quietly executed across five decades, is the harder trick. Family-owned distributors routinely fail to make it past the second generation, let alone the third, especially in a category where scale keeps compounding for everyone else. The tension the About page won't state directly Here is the part of Red Ball's story that a reader would not get from its website: welding gas and industrial gas distribution has spent the last two decades consolidating hard, with multinational strategics absorbing independent regional players across the country. Red Ball has not followed that path. It is still Kennedy-owned, still headquartered in Shreveport, and still small enough that MDM doesn't even list a revenue figure for it, sitting on a Top Distributors ranking dominated by companies that report billions. And yet the company's influence in its own trade association outstrips its balance sheet. Bob Ewing, Red Ball's president, has served as president of GAWDA, the Gases and Welding Distributors Association that represents the entire independent side of this channel, according to industry coverage and the company's own posts referencing him in both current and past-president capacities. That is a specific kind of leverage: a family firm too small to appear on MDM's revenue column has, at points, set the agenda for the trade group that speaks for its national peers. Staying independent didn't mean staying invisible. What the operating model actually looks like Red Ball describes itself as an "open-books, profit-sharing company," a structure that shares financial performance and upside with employees rather than concentrating it in family hands alone, per the company's own about-us materials. That framing matters in a labor-intensive, safety-sensitive business: cylinder handling, bulk gas delivery, and welding equipment service carry real injury risk, and the company has made safety a public metric rather than a private one. In 2025, the Compressed Gas Association gave Red Ball its Distributor Safety Award for companies logging more than 100,000 employee exposure hours, recognizing the greatest safety improvement over a two-year window, with CEO Alex Kennedy accepting at the GAWDA Annual Convention in Tampa. The company also runs two specialty gas laboratories, in Shreveport and Houston, producing certified gas blends for national and international customers under the "Red Ball Technical Gas Services" banner, a business line that sells expertise rather than cylinders and travels well beyond the four-state delivery radius. That's the second half of the model: local branch density and 24/7/365 delivery for the core welding and industrial gas customer, paired with a specialty-chemistry lab business that competes on a completely different, higher-margin axis. Few regional gas distributors run both at once. The bet, restated Red Ball's whole existence rests on one decision made in 1969: get out of batteries and tires, get into gas. Everything since, the fill plants, the specialty labs, the safety record, the GAWDA presidency, the fourth state, is downstream of a single family deciding what business they were actually in. Fifty-six years later the industry around them has consolidated into a handful of giants, and Red Ball is still there, still Kennedy-run, still showing up on the list MDM builds every year to track who's actually moving the freight. Every distributor on that list, family-owned or private-equity-rolled, wins or loses on the same unglamorous infrastructure: the branch network, the fill plant, the delivery truck, and the data that tells all three where to be next. This series looks at how different companies built that infrastructure, and what it cost them to keep it running.

title: Hyundai Elantra Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy
summary: Searching for the definitive Hyundai Elantra buying guide? Our expert overview covers every model generation, with advice on the best and worst versions, and what to look out for if you're buying one.
body_text: When the Hyundai Elantra first appeared, it mainly sold on the basis of its bargain-basement price, and replaced the 1980s Excel in the Korean manufacturer's line-up, slotting in below the larger Sonata. It's been Hyundai's main compact car offering since then and, from the mid-1990s onwards, Hyundai vehicles started to move away from their bargain-bin positioning. Following a merger of Hyundai Motor Group and Kia in 1998, the brand started to get serious about its products. In 1999, Hyundai introduced an impressive 10-year powertrain warranty and, by the arrival of the third-generation Elantra in 2001, it was obvious that Hyundai was taking genuine aim at the established compact market players such as the Toyota Corolla, Nissan Sentra, Honda Civic and Ford Focus. The Elantra has been steadily improving as a product ever since. Most Elantra models over the years have been compact sedans, but you'll also find a two-door coupe, a five-door wagon and a five-door hatchback in the model's history. Power has always come from a four-cylinder engine driving the front wheels alone. It is, in fact, a pretty conservative car, technologically speaking, with the Elantra Hybrid only joining the party relatively late on. The latest Elantra, new in 2021, is among the roomiest and most refined compact cars on the market. In terms of functionality and tech it's up with the best, and it offers lots of choice, including hybrids and a dedicated performance version in the form of the sporty Elantra N. Anyone shopping for a practical, durable, and stylish small car should put the Hyundai Elantra sedan on their shopping list. And the industry-leading warranty? It's now more of a bonus rather than the primary reason to consider the Elantra. Search for Hyundai Elantra See all 2023 Hyundai Elantra $17,525 59,771 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal McAllen, TX 2024 Hyundai Elantra $22,871 19,466 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Tupelo, MS 2024 Hyundai Elantra $22,743 2,900 miles Includes dealer fees Great Deal Jacksonville, AR 2020 Hyundai Elantra $12,978 71,894 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Farmington, NM 2024 Hyundai Elantra $20,670 55,895 miles Includes dealer fees Fair Deal Harlingen, TX 2022 Hyundai Elantra $17,143 57,983 miles Includes dealer fees Good Deal Shawnee, KS Not all Elantras are alike, however, so we've assembled information here about all of this popular compact's generations since 2000. You're unlikely to find very many first- or second-generation 1990s Elantras for sale (at the time of this writing, only one such model, a 2000 sedan, was for sale on CarGurus) and they generate little collector interest, but if you do want one, inspect carefully. They're not as reliable as later versions. Hyundai Elantra Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy Frequently Asked Questions Hyundai Elantra Pros and Cons Hyundai Elantra Generations Seventh Generation (2021-present) Sixth Generation (2017 to 2020) Fifth Generation (2011 to 2016) Fourth Generation (2007 to 2010) Third Generation (2001 to 2006) Frequently Asked Questions Which Hyundai Elantra years are the best? Undoubtedly, the current-generation Elantra, introduced for model year 2021, is the most refined, roomiest, and best-finished of all Elantras. It also offers many different choices. Among older Elantras, the 2007 to 2011 models rate higher for reliability than some newer choices, but the 2009 models seem to have more problems than the others. The hatchback Elantra GT was also less of a known quantity in those years because it was slightly different from the regular models but sold in smaller quantities. 2001 to 2005 models are also durable, and 2018 through 2020 models have above-average repair records according to outlets like Consumer Reports. What are the worst Hyundai Elantra years? 2012 through 2017 models seem to have the worst repair records, but fifth-generation 2012 and 2013 Elantras fare especially poorly, with complaints in lots of areas, mechanical, cosmetic, and electrical. 2017 models also have a below-average reliability record according to outlets like CarComplaints and Consumer Reports, but it isn't as bad as those two earlier years. We don't include the first-generation Elantra in our guide here, but it's also not a quality machine, and we'd steer clear of one so old. How much does a late-model Hyundai Elantra cost? Late-model used Elantras track closely with their age. A 1-year-old 2025 Elantra averages around $21,700, a 3-year-old 2023 model averages around $19,700, and a 5-year-old 2021 example averages around $16,300 on the used market. Research Hyundai Elantra Price Trends on CarGurus Is a used Hyundai Elantra a good deal? Yes, it can be. The Elantra generally costs less than equivalent Honda Civics and Toyota Corollas, though not by much in recent years. Older Elantras also didn't usually offer performance models like Honda's Civic Si or hybrid powertrains. 2011 to 2022 models without push-button starters and engine immobilizers are also particularly vulnerable to theft, which can mean higher than normal insurance rates, negating some of the advantages of their lower prices, but 2001 to 2010 models are cheap to buy and run. Hyundai Elantra Pros and Cons Pros: Plenty of value Great warranty Plenty of room and technology in the current generation Cons: Dull driving dynamics, weak base engines Polarizing styling Some questionable interior materials Hyundai Elantra Generations Seventh Generation (2021-present) In late 2020, the seventh-generation Elantra burst onto the scene with a whole new look and an available hybrid powertrain that returns an EPA fuel efficiency rating of 54 miles per gallon combined. While this latest Elantra dropped the hatchback GT model, it more than made up for this by offering interior room on par with midsize cars of only a few years earlier and by offering many more choices, including a high-performance N model. The core lineup of Hyundai Elantra SE trim, Hyundai Elantra SEL trim, and Hyundai Elantra Limited trim all get a 147-horsepower 2.0-liter four-cylinder mated to a continuously variable transmission (CVT). It's a modest powerplant, but delivers acceptable performance and very good fuel economy of up to 40 mpg on the highway. Elantra Hybrids use a 1.6-liter four and an electric motor with only 139 system horsepower, but gas mileage is even better. The Elantra N-Line looks fast and gets a more powerful 1.6-liter turbocharged four with 201 horsepower mated to a seven-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission. If that's not enough there's also the Elantra N, with a 276-horsepower 2.0-liter turbo and a choice of either a six-speed manual transmission or an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic. It also boasts a variety of handling tweaks that deliver enough of a sporty driving experience to make it a very fun, track-capable machine. CarGurus reviewed the 2022 Hyundai Elantra N and gave it high marks averaging 8.7 out of 10, but all of these latest Elantras handle better than any previous version. Even the earliest, entry-level models have an infotainment system with an 8-inch touchscreen, and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity. Limited trim ups the ante with a larger 10.25-inch touchscreen. Among the generous standard features is Hyundai's SmartSense suite of advanced driver-assistance systems, which includes forward-collision warning with pedestrian detection, blind spot monitoring, automatic emergency braking, lane-departure warning, lane-keeping assist, automatic high beams, and a driver-attention warning system. SEL and upwards feature adaptive cruise control. The trim lineup has changed over the years, with the 2026 model year lineup consisting of SE, SEL Sport, SEL Sport Premium, Limited, N Line, an entry-level Blue trim for the Elantra Hybrid, and the standalone Elantra N. As well as a 5-Year/60,000-mile bumper-to-bumper warranty, the Elantra comes with a 10-Year/100,000-mile powertrain warranty, which provides more peace of mind than you get with many used vehicles. They're also more theft-resistant than the previous generation. It's possible to find low-spec models for as little as $10,000, but newer years and higher trims will run more, with many examples falling between $14,000 and $22,000 at dealerships. On the used market, 2021 models now average around $16,300, while 2025 examples average around $21,700. At the upper end, that's nearly as much as a brand-new 2025 base model. You will get more equipment buying used, but used buyers don't get the full 10-year powertrain warranty. Certified Pre-Owned models are also a great option here, as they come with a little bit more warranty coverage. Elantra Ns are expensive, and as that model has limited availability used, it's probably better to buy one new. Sixth Generation (2017 to 2020) With the sixth-generation Elantra, Hyundai toned down the sedan's polarizing looks in favor of a more conservative and upscale appearance. That didn't last long; A 2019 freshening added dubious geometric shapes that, depending on the trim level and viewing angle, can be downright jarring. Visually, this wasn't Hyundai's strongest effort. It's also easy to get confused by the Elantra GT. 2017 Elantra GTs were leftovers from the previous generation model. For 2018, a completely new and different Elantra GT debuted. Based on the European i30, the Elantra GT is the best version of this car. It looks much nicer and has more room. Fold the rear seats down and cargo space expands from 24.9 to 55.1 cubic feet. Both versions of the sixth-generation Elantra have nicer interiors than ever, modern infotainment and safety features, and and available 201-horsepower 1.6-liter turbocharged engine. Three engine choices are available, but most Elantras have the standard 147-horsepower 2.0-liter four-cylinder with a six-speed manual or conventional automatic transmission. In 2020 a continuously variable transmission (CVT) replaced the automatic in the sedan. Additional choices include a rarely-ordered 128-horsepower 1.4-liter and the punchy 1.6-liter turbo with manual or dual-clutch automatic transmissions, depending on the application. Fuel economy ranges from 25 to 36 mpg in combined driving, depending on powertrain. In 2017, CarGurus gave the Elantra sedan an overall rating of 8.8. A test of the refreshed 2019 Elantra sedan garnered a score of 8.2. Notably, the sixth-gen Elantra sedan and GT earned "Top Safety Pick" or "Top Safety Pick+" designations from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) every year it was on sale. On the negative side, these models are some of the ones that are at the heart of Hyundai's theft vulnerability problem, though there are many steps owners can take to safeguard their cars. Early sixth-gen Elantras can be had for as little as $9,000 in good condition, which is a pretty good deal, though 2017 models don't have a very good reliability record. Models with the 1.6-liter turbo will cost more, but most really nice Elantras in this era range between $11,000 and $17,000. It doesn't seem worthwhile to spend more than $20,000 on one given that there are now plentiful examples of the newer seventh-generation model around for that price. 2018 to 2020 Elantra GTs are harder to find and a little pricier than sedans, but a worthy upgrade. Fifth Generation (2011 to 2016) The dramatically styled fifth-generation Hyundai Elantra first turned heads for the 2011 model year. With its almost sensual body swells, flowing design, and attractive fastback silhouette, the Elantra made buyers take notice, though reactions to such a bold design were mixed. Comparatively, its mechanical twin, the Kia Forte, was a wallflower in the compact car segment. Hyundai also offered the widest range of bodies in the Elantra's history for this generation. The Elantra sedan came out first, joined by a two-door coupe and a five-door hatchback for 2013. The Elantra Coupe was a slow seller and had been discontinued by 2015. The Elantra GT hatchback, replacing the previous Elantra Touring, remained available through 2017, overlapping with the sixth-generation sedans. This time, the Elantra GT was much closer to the sedan in style and feel than the Touring had been or the later 2018 model would be. In 2011 and 2012, that old Elantra Touring continued prior to the debut of the hatchback GT. That model is rare, but among the best buys in these years. A 148-horsepower, 1.8-liter four-cylinder engine was standard, paired with a manual or automatic transmission. In 2014, Hyundai added a more powerful 2.0-liter four-cylinder that made 173 hp. Fuel economy ranged from 27 to 31 mpg combined. As with the subsequent sixth generation, the fifth-gen Elantra earned good marks for safety, though it didn't clinch quite as many IIHS "Top Safety Pick" awards as its successor. Though it had few recalls, this version of the Elantra has a mixed reliability record. Some sources like the Dashboard Light index, give it pretty average ratings, while others, like Consumer Reports and CarComplaints, rate it the worst of all Elantra generations since 2000. 2012 and 2013 models seem to come in for particular criticism across the board, with complaints about the electrical and HVAC systems, suspensions, engines, brakes, and overall build quality. These models are also some of the most theft-vulnerable Elantras. The good news is, they're cheap. Elantra Tourings from these years can be found in good shape with under 70,000 miles for about $8,000. The very best and lowest-mile sedans can cost up to about $14,000, but it's easy to find good ones for $6,500 to $10,000. All things considered, the 2011-2012 Touring models are the best of the lot. Fourth Generation (2007 to 2010) Building on the success of the third generation, the fourth-generation model arrived for the 2007 model year. At first, the fourth-generation Elantra was only available as a five-passenger sedan, but starting in 2009, a hatchback called the Elantra Touring arrived. Based on the European Hyundai i30, it boasted more enjoyable driving dynamics and remained in production through the 2012 model year. The Elantra Touring is both better looking than the anonymous sedan and more useful since it's basically a small station wagon and not dissimilar to some modern subcompact crossovers. All fourth-generation Elantras had a 138-horsepower, 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine with a manual or automatic transmission. Fuel economy ranged from 26 to 32 mpg in combined driving. For 2010, Hyundai introduced a Blue trim level marketed as a more eco-friendly version of the sedan, but all it did was bump the highway fuel economy number from 34 to 35 mpg—and it only managed that with the manual transmission. The fourth-generation Elantra proved to be fairly reliable, too, though complaints seem to center on the braking system and premature brake wear. There was a fuel pump recall in 2008, and the 2008-10 models saw recalls for power steering, but these models are fairly trouble-free, with the best repair record of any Elantra generation according to some sources, including Dashboard Light. They're also not any more vulnerable to theft than their contemporaries like the Nissan Sentra or Ford Focus. They're not very exciting to drive though, or look at, and they don't have as many features as later Elantras. Given that the newest of these are now 14 years old, they're getting harder to find. They're very affordable though, and good examples with under 80,000 miles on the odometer should cost only about $6,000 to $9,000. The Touring may sell for a little more, and it continued into 2012, so if you like it, there are a few newer ones to try out. They don't cost much more, either. Third Generation (2001 to 2006) It wasn't until Hyundai introduced the third-generation Elantra that people started taking the company's vehicles seriously. In part, that was down to word of mouth about Hyundai's lengthy new warranty (which had debuted in 1999), but also because of the many improvements made to this Elantra versus its predecessor. While some buyers lamented the discontinuance of the former Elantra station wagon, most people liked the new car's more sophisticated look and feel. Admittedly, the third-generation Elantra wasn't the best-looking compact car you could buy at the time, but its workhorse nature was enough to turn Hyundai's reputation around. It also came along at a time when Honda and Toyota seemed to lose interest in materially improving their competing offerings, so the Elantra looked much better in comparison to the Civic and Corolla than it had in previous generations, even if it still had plenty of "cheap car" stigma leftover from the 1990s. Hyundai also made many more features standard, including a passenger's side airbag, power locks, air conditioning, power steering, and power windows. First introduced as a sedan for 2001, the new Elantra lineup gained a five-door hatchback for 2002. Both had a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine with a manual or automatic transmission and were, of course, front-wheel drive (FWD). The third-gen Elantra kept this engine all through its run, with only minor changes in horsepower ratings and tuning (they all made between 135 and 140 horsepower). In spite of its impressive warranty, earlier versions of the third-generation Elantra were recalled several times for braking, suspension, and fuel tank issues pertaining to the 2001-2003 models. A few airbag problems popped up, too, but they were unrelated to the massive Takata airbag recall. In general, however, the repair record was much better than the first two generations, and the car more durable in the long term. In places where cars don't rust, you can still find plenty of them commuting around, though age has reduced their numbers. They're cheap if you can find them though, and even really nice ones generally don't cost more than $6,000. If you really need a bargain-basement commuter, it's not a terrible choice, though not much more will buy you newer examples of Civics and Corollas. body_text: Financial stress has long been associated with poor mental and physical health, but growing evidence suggests it may also affect brain health over time. Recent research indicates that people who experience long-term financial hardship may face a greater risk of faster brain aging, cognitive decline, and potentially Alzheimer's disease. While occasional money worries are common, persistent financial struggles appear to have a much deeper impact. Researchers say that chronic economic hardship can create long-lasting stress that affects the brain's ability to process information, make decisions, and maintain memory as people age. In this article, we explore what the latest research reveals about the connection between financial stress and brain health, why some people may be more vulnerable, and what these findings could mean for public health. Financial Hardship and Brain Health Researchers have increasingly focused on the relationship between socioeconomic conditions and cognitive health. Rather than examining a person's financial situation at one point in time, newer studies have tracked individuals over several decades. The findings suggest that people who experience ongoing financial hardship during early and middle adulthood tend to perform worse on cognitive assessments later in life. Brain imaging has also revealed signs of poorer brain health among those who spent many years living on lower incomes. This does not mean that financial difficulties directly cause dementia. Instead, the evidence points to a strong association between prolonged economic hardship and factors linked to cognitive aging. Why Chronic Financial Stress Matters Money problems often create ongoing stress that extends beyond paying monthly bills. Long-term financial insecurity can affect nearly every aspect of daily life, including: Sleep quality Mental health Nutrition Physical activity Access to healthcare Social participation Chronic stress activates the body's stress response repeatedly. Over time, elevated stress hormones may affect areas of the brain responsible for learning, memory, attention, and decision making. Researchers believe this continuous pressure may gradually reduce the brain's resilience, making cognitive decline more likely later in life. Who May Face Greater Risk? Although financial hardship can affect anyone, research suggests that certain groups may experience stronger effects. These include: Men Individuals who experienced socioeconomic disadvantage during childhood People with a higher genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease Experts believe that genetics and lifelong environmental factors may work together, influencing how the brain responds to prolonged stress. Importantly, having a genetic risk does not guarantee someone will develop Alzheimer's disease. Lifestyle, overall health, education, and environmental factors all contribute to brain health. Brain Aging Is Influenced by Many Factors Brain aging is a complex process. Financial stress is only one piece of a much larger puzzle. Other well-established risk factors for cognitive decline include: High blood pressure Diabetes Smoking Physical inactivity Obesity Depression Social isolation Hearing loss Poor sleep Excessive alcohol consumption Many of these factors can be improved through lifestyle changes and appropriate medical care. The Cost of Chronic Stress Living with persistent financial insecurity often requires constant decision making about housing, food, transportation, and healthcare. Experts sometimes describe this as reducing a person's mental bandwidth. When the brain is continually focused on immediate financial concerns, fewer cognitive resources may remain for planning, learning, memory, and problem solving. Although everyone experiences stress differently, long-term exposure may contribute to cumulative wear on the brain over many years. Why the Findings Matter As populations continue to age, dementia has become one of the world's most significant public health challenges. Research increasingly shows that preventing dementia is not only about healthcare. Social and economic conditions also play an important role. Policies that reduce poverty, improve access to education, strengthen employment opportunities, and provide financial support during difficult times may benefit overall brain health across the population. These findings reinforce the idea that improving social conditions could have positive health effects that extend well beyond financial wellbeing. Can You Reduce Your Risk? While no strategy can completely prevent Alzheimer's disease or other forms of dementia, experts recommend focusing on healthy lifestyle habits that support brain health. These include: Staying physically active Eating a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats Managing blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes Getting adequate sleep Avoiding smoking Limiting excessive alcohol intake Staying socially connected Challenging the brain through lifelong learning and mentally stimulating activities Seeking support for chronic stress, anxiety, or depression If financial stress is affecting your wellbeing, speaking with a financial adviser, community support organization, or healthcare professional may also help reduce its long-term impact. Looking Ahead Scientists continue to investigate how financial hardship influences brain aging over the course of a lifetime. Future studies may help identify which interventions are most effective at protecting cognitive health among people facing economic challenges. The growing body of evidence highlights that brain health is shaped by more than genetics and medical care. Social circumstances, economic stability, education, and access to resources all contribute to healthy aging. Supporting individuals experiencing long-term financial hardship may therefore benefit not only their immediate quality of life but also their cognitive health in later years. Final Thoughts Financial stress is more than an economic issue. It can influence physical health, mental wellbeing, and potentially the way the brain ages over time. While researchers continue to study this connection, the evidence suggests that reducing chronic financial hardship could become an important part of future dementia prevention efforts. Although financial challenges cannot always be avoided, adopting healthy lifestyle habits, managing stress where possible, and ensuring access to healthcare and social support remain valuable steps toward maintaining brain health throughout life. If you have concerns about memory problems, cognitive decline, dementia risk, or your overall health, consult a qualified healthcare professional. Research findings show associations and do not necessarily establish direct cause and effect.
